final.title: Privacy promises do not control your workflow
final.body:
If you are thinking about AI in a small business, privacy promises are only part of the picture. A vendor can explain data storage, encryption, or terms of use, but that still does not answer the operational question that matters inside your own business: who is allowed to act on the data once it enters the workflow?

That is the bounded decision I would make first. For any repeatable process, such as invoice handling or customer replies, decide whether the AI may take action on its own, or whether it only recommends an action and waits for human approval. For money movement and other high-risk decisions, human approval stays mandatory. That is Bareni policy, not a clever slogan.

Privacy expectations do not enforce your approval process. If the workflow is loose, a strong privacy statement does not fix that. If the workflow is tight, you can use AI without handing over the keys to the shop.

A simple diagnostic question helps: will I see the input, the reasoning, and the recommended action before anything is committed?

Next, map your most repeated workflow, mark the points where money, customer communication, or data deletion could happen, and decide which of those points must remain human-approved.
